common_name: Blackwell Switchgrass (Historic Oklahoma Upland Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Blackwell was selected from a single native prairie plant found near Blackwell, Oklahoma, and released in 1944, making it one of the oldest switchgrass cultivars still in commerce.

directions: Blackwell is a classic upland switchgrass ecotype developed by the Soil Conservation Service from a single Oklahoma prairie plant collected in 1934, and it remains one of the most disease-resistant, leafy switchgrass selections available for conservation and native landscape plantings. It stays more moderate in height and spread than the giant lowland cultivars, forming a dense, upright clump of blue-green summer foliage that fades to warm gold-tan through fall and winter. Its heavy leafiness and rust resistance made it a mainstay of Great Plains pasture and erosion-control seedings for decades, and those same traits translate into a tidy, long-lived garden plant that needs no supplemental water once rooted. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new shoots emerge.

common_name: Carthage Switchgrass (North Carolina Lowland Ecotype Switchgrass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Carthage traces to a single lowland-type plant collected near Carthage, North Carolina, and is regionally adapted to the warm, humid conditions of the Southeast.

directions: Carthage is a Southeastern lowland switchgrass ecotype that forms tall, robust clumps of coarse blue-green blades well suited to the long, humid growing season of the coastal plain and Piedmont. Because it descends from a moisture-loving parent plant, it handles occasional wet feet and periodic flooding along ditches, pond edges, and rain gardens better than upland switchgrass selections, while still tolerating average garden soil once established. Loose, airy seed panicles open in late summer atop the tall foliage and age to warm gold, remaining a source of winter interest and songbird forage through the cold months. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches above the ground in late winter before spring growth resumes.

common_name: Kaw Big Bluestem (Flint Hills Prairie Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average, dry soil in full sun; Kaw was developed from over 200 accessions gathered from the Flint Hills tallgrass prairie south of Manhattan, Kansas, and released in 1950.

directions: Kaw is a taller, later-maturing, and more uniformly leafy big bluestem release than typical wild-collected seed, bred from Flint Hills prairie stock for forage volume and dependable seed production, traits that also give it exceptional presence as a back-of-border prairie grass. Reddish-purple summer stems carry the species' signature blue-green foliage before turning a rich copper-orange in fall and holding as tan winter straw. The three-pronged, turkey-foot seed heads appear in late summer and add strong vertical texture through the dormant season. Established clumps are extremely drought tolerant thanks to deep prairie roots and need no irrigation or fertilizer once settled; cut the plant back to about 6 inches in early spring before new growth begins.

common_name: Lometa Indiangrass (Texas Native Grass for Central and South Texas)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lometa was released by the Texas Plant Materials Center from central and south Texas ecotypes and outperforms other indiangrass releases in that hot, variable climate.

directions: Lometa is a Texas-bred indiangrass selection prized for staying in vegetative growth longer into early summer than most warm-season natives, a habit that keeps its blue-green foliage lush and useful before the tall, golden-bronze flower plumes rise on wiry stems in early fall. Bred specifically for resilience across the heat, drought swings, and variable soils of central and south Texas, it is a dependable, low-input choice for Gulf Coast and Texas native meadow plantings where many other indiangrass sources struggle to persist. Foliage shifts from cool blue-green through the growing season to warm tan by winter, and the seed heads feed native birds through the cold months. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program (Knox City, Texas)

common_name: Verl Eastern Gamagrass (Triploid Pasture and Wildlife Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately wet soil in full sun; Verl was released in 2005 by USDA-ARS with the Oklahoma Agricultural Experiment Station and NRCS and is recommended for the eastern and southern United States.

directions: Verl is a distinctive eastern gamagrass release that reproduces largely through apomixis, meaning seedlings grow true to the parent type rather than showing the wide variability typical of gamagrass grown from open-pollinated seed. It forms dense, long-lived clumps of broad, corn-like leaves topped by jointed summer seed spikes, and was developed specifically for reliable pasture and hay performance across the warm, humid conditions of the southern and eastern states. In the landscape it brings bold, tropical-looking texture to rain gardens, pond margins, and moist native meadows, tolerating seasonal flooding and heavy soils better than most warm-season grasses. Mow or graze carefully to avoid cutting into the low growing point, which can set the clump back for a full season; otherwise it needs little care once established.

common_name: Pete Eastern Gamagrass (Widely Adapted Prairie and Forage Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pete was released in 1988 from a composite of roughly 70 native gamagrass populations gathered across Kansas and Oklahoma and closely resembles wild-type stands.

directions: Pete is a broadly adapted eastern gamagrass release bred from dozens of wild prairie populations rather than a single parent plant, giving it genetic diversity and resilience close to naturally occurring stands. Dense clumps of wide, arching, corn-like leaves rise from a slow-spreading crown, and jointed seed spikes appear in summer bearing large, hard seeds that were historically ground into flour and remain valuable forage for deer, turkey, and other wildlife. It establishes slowly from divisions in its first year or two but becomes a long-lived, low-maintenance fixture of moist meadows, bottomland plantings, and bioswales once rooted in. Its bold texture and deep-green color make a strong contrast planted among finer-bladed native grasses; cut clumps back in late winter before new growth begins.
